CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Wards
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
A ward is one ring of the settlement. A market town has three: the old town behind the high wall, the suburb behind a lighter one, and the open countryside around them.
Everything else hangs off a ward. Its wall, its towers, its gatehouses, and the districts that decide what gets built inside it.
The order in the list is the order from the middle outwards. The innermost ward is the one the generator protects best and fills first, so put what matters there.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Districts
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
A district is a group of buildings inside a ward, for example a market quarter or a row of farmsteads.
Each row is either a category or one specific piece, with a count. Priority decides which row gets room first; Low rows may stay below their minimum when the space runs out. A Filler row fills the room left at the end. Weight only counts for a single piece, against the other pieces of its category.
Fields and pens belong to a district too. That is how the generator knows a farmstead gets fields and a tavern does not.
Location of the district sets where it starts: near the center, near the gate, near the wall or on the main road. Nothing ticked means a random spot away from the other districts.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Walls
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The wall pieces this ward is built from. The generator picks from the list whenever it needs a stretch of wall, so several entries give a wall that varies along its length.
Depth is how thick the ring is. One is a palisade, three is a town wall with a rampart walk on top.
Where a mountain meets the line, the mountain is the wall and nothing is built in front of it.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Field emplacements
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Towers and other defensive works that sit in the wall ring.
The generator spaces them along the wall by itself, at the corners first and then along the long straight runs. How many fit follows from the length of the wall, not from a number you set here.
The size of the largest tower in this list also sets how much room the planner reserves at every corner, so a very large tower makes the whole outline coarser.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Gatehouses
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Where a road crosses the wall, a gatehouse is built.
The number follows from the roads, not from a setting. The planner lays out the approach roads first and puts a gate wherever one has to pass through the ring, then checks that every gate can actually be reached from outside.
A piece used here needs a passable opening. Without one the ward is sealed and the whole layout is discarded.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Anchors
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
An anchor is a marked area inside a piece where something happens once the piece is placed.
Connect anchors tie the piece to its surroundings. Wall is where the town wall docks, Outside tells which side faces out, Annex is where annexes attach.
Loot anchors place objects from an object list and fill them from a loot table. Object anchors place objects from an object list with a chance, without loot. Pawn anchors bring in people or animals from a pawn list, with a role that decides whether they stay and fight or run.
An anchor whose list does not exist marks the piece red in the editor.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Farmland
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Crop plots and animal pens for the open countryside.
A crop plot is grown around a rural building, not dropped on the map at random. Which buildings get one is decided by the district the plot is listed under. Min and max bound how many plots that building may have.
A pen holds one kind of animal, drawn from a unit list. The herd size is the second row, indented under the pen.
Both get a fence with one gate. Where rock or water already closes the line, no fence is built in front of it.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Settlement plans per faction
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Which of your settlement plans are used when the player walks into a base of this faction.
The assignment is not stored on the faction. It is stored as factionTags inside the plan, and the generator collects every plan whose tags match the faction. Two mods can therefore both serve the same faction without either one overwriting the other.
A plan that names no faction at all serves every faction. That is why a fresh plan shows up everywhere until you assign it.
Removing works only for plans attached by faction name. A plan attached through the faction category has to be detached in the plan itself.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Takeover
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Nothing you assign here shows up until RimWorld actually hands faction bases to this generator. That is what the takeover switch does.
It writes one patch file into the Patches folder of the current mod. The patch swaps a single generation step, Settlement for CBF_Settlement, and leaves everything else in place, so faction bases keep their rocks and their power lines.
If a patch file is already there, the operation is added to it and the rest of the file is kept. Switching the takeover off removes only that operation, not the file, unless nothing else is left in it.
A faction with no matching plan falls back to RimWorld's own settlement, never to an empty map.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Annexes
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
An annex is a small piece that attaches to a house: a stable, a woodshed, a beer garden. Everything about it is data in the categories and pieces, nothing is fixed in code.
Annex categories on the house's category say which annexes may attach to it. An empty list takes the list of the parent category.
Chance per anchor is the chance that an annex is built at one annex anchor of the house, default 0.6. At most caps the number of annexes per house, default 2.
Repeatable belongs on the category of the annex itself. Yes allows the same annex several times on one house.
Weight decides which annex is picked when several fit. For annexes, a weight below 1 is also the chance that this annex is tried at all.
The anchor is a Connect anchor named Annex. On the house it lies on the outer wall. On the annex it lies either on its outer wall, when both share that wall, or one cell outside its shape, when the annex only touches the house.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: At the wall
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
How much a piece wants to stand against the town wall. The planner reads it when it places buildings.
Forbidden keeps the piece away from the wall. Avoid, Allowed, Preferred and Strongly preferred weigh the spots along the wall lower or higher. Required forces contact: the piece is only placed where it touches the wall.
A piece without a value of its own takes the wall contact of its category. Yes there means Preferred.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Ward door
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The door that closes the passages through this ward's wall, for example a wooden door for a palisade.
Empty uses the door of the material list of the settlement type, which is what most wards want. The gatehouse is something else, it is set under Fortification.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Placement
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Where buildings of this category may stand. Every value is inherited from the parent category until set here.
Road access: buildings of this category must be reachable from the road network.
Needs no road only takes effect when Road access is No. Buildings of this category then need no road and may be entered from every side, like a farm or a market.
Wall contact: pieces of this category prefer to stand against the town wall. The piece field At the wall controls this more finely and wins.
Weight: how often pieces of this category are drawn when several fit. 1 is normal. For annexes, a value below 1 is also the chance that the annex is tried at all.
How many buildings of a category a settlement gets is set by its entries in the Settlement tab.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Blocks
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
A block is a row of buildings that stand wall to wall.
Block limit: how many buildings of this category at most form one block. Empty means 3.
Merge: whether buildings of this category join their neighbours into one block. Yes forces it, No forbids it.
The generator reads both values only from the building's own first category, not from its parents.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Used in
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Every settlement type and dungeon that names this category somewhere in its plan.
A line says where: in a district of a ward, in the fortification, on a dungeon level or in one of its sections, corridors, stairs or decoration. Districts also show the count they ask for.
Click a line to open that plan. A category that no plan names can still be built through a child category or a parent category that a plan asks for.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Affects
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Where this loot table ends up in the game.
Directly part of: the tables that draw this one, with the weight they give it, or always when it sits under Always included. Click one to open it.
Through pieces in settlements: the settlement types that reach this table through their pieces, with those pieces named.
The tiles below show every piece that uses the table, directly at an anchor or through an object list. The anchors that use it are highlighted. Click a tile to open the piece.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Gear
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The apparel this pawn kind always wears.
The grid shows the apparel layers in rows, from outside in, and the body parts in columns. Click a free cell to pick only what fits there. Hatched cells are blocked by the gear of the same colour. Hide empty hides rows and columns nobody uses.
The list below the grid shows each piece with layer, material, quality and colour. Swap replaces a piece with another one that fits the same layers and keeps material, quality and colour where possible.
The most advanced piece of gear sets the tech level of the pawn kind, and that decides in which settlements it appears.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Weapon
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Which weapon the pawn gets.
Tags are the weapon tags RimWorld draws from, for example a group of bows. Budget is the silver value the weapon may cost, as a range. Quality and Weapon material narrow the result further. Empty means any.
The weapon also counts towards the tech level of the pawn kind.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Skills
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Skill levels the pawn starts with.
Each row sets a range for one skill. Min. best: the best skill reaches at least this level. Min. total: all skill levels together reach at least this value. Extra levels are spread at random on top.
Skills not named here are rolled by RimWorld as usual.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Nature
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Traits the pawn may not have and traits it always gets.
Forbidden traits are never rolled. Forced traits are always given, with their degree where the trait has one. Everything else is rolled by RimWorld as usual.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Implants
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Bionics and other implants the pawn spawns with.
Fixed implants are always installed. Tags and Budget let RimWorld pick further implants with those tags up to that silver value, with the chance and at most the count set here.
An implant shown in red cannot be installed in this race and is skipped at spawn.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: All fields
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Every field of the pawn kind that the sections above do not cover, sorted into groups.
Changes here go into the same file as the rest. An empty field keeps the value RimWorld or the parent pawn kind gives it.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Check results
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
What the last check found wrong with this piece.
Red lines are errors. While there are errors, the piece cannot be exported. The other lines are notes and block nothing, for example a gatehouse that still lacks its Wall anchor.
Check at the bottom runs the check again. While the piece is on the map it checks what is built there, otherwise the saved file.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Basics
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
What the piece is and where it may be used.
Size and Categories: the first category is the main one. Settlements ask for categories, so a piece without one is never built.
Rotation allowed lets the generator turn the piece. Clear footprint removes whatever stands under the piece before it is built. At the wall and Weight only apply to buildings: how much the piece wants to stand against the town wall, and how often it is drawn among the pieces of its category.
Only with mod and Off with mod tie the piece to other mods. Only for factions and Not for factions do the same for factions.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Derived
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Values the editor works out by itself. They cannot be set here.
Type is Building, WallPart or DungeonRoom. It follows from the main category when the piece is exported. Buildings go into districts, wall parts into the wall ring, dungeon rooms into dungeon levels.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Fortification
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The ring around this ward.
Walls: the wall pieces of the ring. Several entries give a wall that varies along its length; the slider sets each entry's share.
Emplacements: towers and other works in the ring. The generator spaces them by itself, corners first.
Gatehouses: built wherever a road crosses the wall.
Door: closes the passages through the wall. Empty uses the door of the material list.
The countryside has no ring. Modern towns use sandbags or barricades and never get gatehouses.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Garrison
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The defenders of this ward or dungeon level.
Each row names a pawn list with a min and max count and a post: Inside, Wall or Gate. The header shows the points of the whole garrison.
With a garrison factor set under General, each row gets an active tick and a weight. Only active rows place fixed pawns: min first, then more up to max by weight while the budget lasts. The rest comes from the faction.
A ward without rows takes its share of the settlement's points. Pawns from Pawn anchors in the pieces come on top.
Every ward defends itself. Guards on the wall and at the gates hold their spot, gun crews stay at their gun.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Roads and ground
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The surfaces of this ward.
Ground: the ground between the houses. Empty keeps the map's own ground.
Paths: the surface of lanes, squares and gate passages. Empty uses the road of the material list.
Kerb: the surface of the outermost cells of lanes, squares and gate passages. Empty uses the path surface for the whole width.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Rules of other mods
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Swap rules that other mods bring for this faction. They are shown here and never changed.
For each unit or thing, the rule with the highest priority wins. Rules with the same priority are combined and drawn by weight.
To override another mod for one unit, give your own rule a higher priority.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Basics
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
What the place looks like.
Label is the name players see. Kind of place switches between medieval town, modern town, camp and mountain city. Material list sets the walls, doors, gates, fences and roads the generator builds by itself; without one the type is switched off.
Map size, Core size and Tree share set how much room the place takes and how many wild trees stay. Rock mantle is the mountain around a mountain city.
Build as ruin, Ideoligion style, the suburb settings and the world map icon finish the look.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Placement
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Who gets this settlement type and where it appears.
Tech levels: which ages the plan fits. For all factions of these levels serves every faction of a ticked level that has no plan of its own. Factions adds factions by name, Excluded keeps factions away.
Weight: how often this type is picked among all types a faction can get.
Ideoligion has and lacks, Biomes, Hilliness and Landforms limit the type to factions and tiles where all set conditions apply. Empty means anywhere.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Garrison
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
How many defenders the whole place has.
Minimum points are always spent on defenders. The garrison factor multiplies the raid points of your colony; the place spends that, but never less than the minimum. With 0, the garrison rows of the wards work as fixed counts.
Pawn anchors count against the budget: how much of the points of anchored pawns is taken from it. Share per ward spreads the bought defenders over the wards, by size or by hand.
Calculate garrison shows per ward what a chosen faction gets at chosen raid points.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Mods
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Settings that tie the settlement type to other mods.
WD tier, WD type and RIAF holding only appear when World Domination or A Rim of Ice and Fire are active. They make this type the plan for their settlements. Camp types only appear for camps and name the quest sites this plan builds.
Takeover hands faction bases to CBF. Mods lists the mods the plan needs. Most are found by themselves, + by hand adds more.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Sections
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
A level can be split into sections that lie one behind the other, for example a front part and a back part. The generator builds them in this order.
The first section is marked entrance: the way in lies there. On the first level that is the entrance from the surface, on lower levels the stairs up. The last section is marked stairs down: the stairs to the next level are built there. Which pieces they are is set under Entrance and stairs. The arrows change the order, and with it which section holds the entrance and which the stairs.
Each section has its own areas. It can also have its own corridor segments and corridor decor; empty means it uses those of the level.
A level without sections uses its own areas.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Entrance and stairs
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The rooms that connect this level to the outside and to the next level.
Entrance, only on the first level: the room with the way in from the surface. Empty means the generator opens a plain tunnel into the mountain. On lower levels the stairs up are placed exactly where the stairs down of the level above stand.
Stairs down: the room with the stairs to the next level. Every level except the lowest needs one. A stair piece needs a Connect anchor named StairsDown, the way up one named StairsUp; it marks where the passage between the maps lies.
With sections, the entrance lies in the first section and the stairs down in the last.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Passages
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
How the rooms of this level are connected.
Layout decides the arrangement, for example corridors, chambers, a cave or a temple. With several ticked, each generated level rolls one of them.
Corridor segments: the pieces the corridors are built from, by share. The strip shows the corridor in order, with the corridor decor on top.
Cave width and Cave share set how wide the cave passages are and how many connections become natural cave instead of built corridor. Secret passages is the chance that a door that would be bricked up gets a hidden passage instead.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Corridor decor
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
Things placed along the corridors: torches, candles, bones, runners.
They stand on the corridor floor against the wall, on both sides at random. Wall fixtures such as torches face the wall, everything else faces into the corridor. Edge and Road make no difference here.
Each row names an object list, a piece or a category, with the spacing between two placements and at most how many per level. The templates add a row with fitting values. The strip above, at the corridor segments, shows the result.
A section without decor of its own uses the decor of the level.

CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.label: Areas
CustomBaseFramework.HelpDef.description:
The rooms of this level, grouped like the districts of a ward.
Each row is a category or one specific piece, with a count. Priority decides which row gets room first; Low rows may stay below their minimum when the space runs out. An area can bring its own layout.
With sections, every section has its own areas.
